en: The Ten Gates of Non-duality,
composed by the Venerable Master Zhànrán of Jīngxī during the Táng Dynasty.
This Trace Gate discusses its causes and effects, as well as the self and others, so that the teachings of a lifetime may [be understood].
Because they are integrated and enter the wondrous.
All explanations of these meanings are based upon the four teachings and the five flavors; the intent is to open up the teachings so that all may enter the *t'ien-mu* (ghee).

Contemplating the mind is the pivotal mechanism of both teaching and practice; however, it has been briefly indicated here, appearing only intermittently within various expositions. As this is not the primary intent of the [specific] section, even where there are established arrangements based on phenomena or principles, they merely serve to distinguish the ten contemplations by listing their names.

The principles and objects clarified, the wisdom and practices, and the stages and dharmas—whether the capacity to transform or those to be transformed—all have their intent in the means of expression (*abhilāpa*), and within these expressions, all are wondrous.

To distinguish the beginning and end, as well as the self and others, within these expressions, the ten wondrousnesses (*daśa-vaipulya*) are fully expounded to encompass the entirety of the Buddha’s transformation of beings. Since the great purport of his appearance in the world is exhaustively revealed therein, one must not fail to understand the general outline of the ten wondrousnesses; therefore, the ten wondrousnesses are summarized here as the fundamental framework for the method of contemplation.
If one understands that the subtlety of the trace is such that the subtlety of the origin is not remote, one should know that there is only a difference between separation and union.
Since the meaning of cause and effect is one, how can self and other be distinct?
Therefore, the text below states: "Though origin and trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability."

Moreover, since essence, doctrine, and function are merely the phenomena of cause and effect between self and other, and since the aspects of the teaching are merely the differentiation of the preceding four chapters—such that the preceding four chapters would stand forever distinct from all other texts—if one understands this principle, then the teaching will have its proper destination.

Throughout a single kalpa, all that is transverse and vertical does not transcend the one mind; the three thousandfold world is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. From the principle and the realm down to benefit for others, it is all thus. Consequently, the ten stages of cessation and contemplation constitute the causes and effects of one’s own practice in the present;
the chapter on "Arousing the Teaching" constitutes the agent and object of transforming others in the present.

Thus, both [the principle and the practice] become clearly manifest, the practice of the Lotus Sūtra is perfected, ensuring that one's efforts are not in vain, and that which is expounded can be understood.
Therefore, the ten profundities are further subsumed within ten gates.

Why is this? When the provisional is established for the sake of the real, the non-dual becomes dual; when the provisional is opened to reveal the real, the dual becomes non-dual. Since both the Dharma and its teachings have been fully opened to become wondrous, these ten gates are titled "Non-Duality," and beneath each gate, one examines them by means of the six stages of realization.

In the preceding section on the Essential Gate, I have already extensively cited authentic proofs; from here below, I shall simply set forth the single principle directly, so that the purport of this entire scripture may shine clearly before one’s eyes.

These are: first, the gate of the non-duality of form and mind; second, the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external; third, the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature; fourth, the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect; fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity; sixth, the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants; seventh, the gate of the non-duality of self and others; eighth, the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas; ninth, the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real; and tenth, the gate of the non-duality of receiving and moistening.
Among these, the first is named according to the excellence of its object;
the second and third are named according to their wisdom and practice;
and the fourth is named according to its stage and dharmas.
The fifth, sixth, and seventh are named according to their responsive spiritual powers;
the eighth and ninth are named according to their preaching of the Dharma;
and the tenth is named according to the benefits conferred upon its retinue.

First, regarding the Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind: from the ten suchnesses of objects up to the ultimate truth, each may be understood through both the general and specific perspectives. Generally, they are unified within a single thought-moment; specifically, they are distinguished as matter and mind.

Why is this? Among the first ten aspects (*lakṣaṇa*), characteristics (*nimitta*) pertain exclusively to form (*rūpa*), while nature (*svabhāva*) pertains exclusively to mind (*citta*). Essence (*tattva*), power (*bala*), activity (*kriyā*), and conditions (*pratyaya*) encompass both form and mind; causes (*hetu*) and fruits (*phala*) pertain exclusively to mind; and retribution (*vipāka*) pertains exclusively to form.

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), suffering (*duḥkha*) and karma (*karman*) pertain to both, while afflictions (*kleśa*) pertain exclusively to mind.
Regarding the Four Truths: three of them involve both matter and mind, while Cessation pertains only to the mind;
regarding the Two Truths and Three Truths: all are conventional and possess both matter and mind, whereas the True and the Middle are mind-only;
the One Reality and Non-existence may be understood by analogy with this.

Once the distinctions have been known, these distinctions are subsumed into the whole: all phenomena (*dharmas*) are none other than the nature of mind. Within this single nature that is "no-nature," the three thousand worlds are manifest.

One should know that the "matter" of the mind is simply the mind; this is called "transformation. Transformation is termed "creation"; creation refers to essence and function. Thus, it is neither matter nor mind, yet it appears as matter and mind; that it is "only matter" and "only mind" truly arises from this.
Therefore, know that by simply recognizing a single thought-moment, one universally perceives the Buddhas and sentient beings of both oneself and others.

If the sentient beings and Buddhas of others are already identical to one’s own mind, how much more so must the sentient beings and Buddhas arising from one's own mind not deviate from this single thought-moment?
Therefore, regarding those various objective dharmas, they are both differentiated and non-differentiated.

Second, the Gate of the Non-duality of Internal and External: whatever objects are contemplated do not transcend the internal and the external. "External" refers to relying upon the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind; these are immediately emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle, and because this immediate emptiness, provisionality, and Middle are wondrous, the essence of form and mind is utterly transcendent.

In the single true nature, there is neither emptiness, the provisional, nor the middle; yet form and mind are vividly present, suddenly identical with true purity. There are no longer distinctions between sentient beings and the seven stages of the expedient means, nor is one seen to perceive differences in the purity or defilement of lands; nevertheless, the Indra’s net of the environment and its inhabitants remains forever brilliantly manifest.

Regarding what is called "internal": first, one realizes that external forms and the mind are, in a single thought-moment, devoid of discursive thought; there is only the internal essence of the three thousand [realms] as emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle. Thus, external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind.

The nature of the mind has no exterior; its encompassing is all-pervasive. The Buddhas of the ten directions, the dharma-realm, and sentient beings—there is no difference in their essential nature, and it universally pervades all. Who, then, can speak of inner and outer, matter and mind, self and other?
This is accomplished by means of the aforementioned "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind. Third, regarding the "Gate of the Non-duality of Practice and Nature":

The nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*) is simply the realm of suchness (*dharmadhātu*) within a single thought-moment; within this internal realm of suchness, the three factors are fully present. Although the nature is thus from the beginning, one relies upon wisdom to initiate practice. Through practice, one illuminates the nature; through the nature, one gives rise to practice. If one abides in the nature, then the entirety of practice becomes the nature; if one initiates practice, then the entirety of the nature becomes practice. The nature does not shift, yet practice remains ever manifest.
Cultivation is further of two kinds:
cultivation in accordance with [the nature] and cultivation contrary to it.
"In accordance" means that understanding one's nature constitutes practice; "contrary" means turning one's back on that nature and becoming deluded.
There are two states of delusion and enlightenment; though the mind itself is not dual, its two natures—contrary and compliant—are eternally distinct in their manifestations.

While the manifestations may shift, the mind does not move; thus, it causes delusion to become realization and cultivation to reach completion. Therefore, one must undergo this single period of delusion and enlightenment: by illuminating the nature to perfect cultivation, and seeing the nature to cultivate the mind, both states of mind are extinguished.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of the cultivation that accords with [the path], there is both separation and combination. "Separation" refers to the three types of each for cultivation and nature; "combination" refers to two for cultivation and one for nature.
Since the two cultivations each have three and together give rise to the three natures, although cultivation possesses nine aspects, these nine are merely three.

Because one practices for the sake of clarifying the nature, the two types of cultivation are combined; these two and the single nature are like water and its waves—the two are non-dual, just as waves are not separate from water.

One should know that "nature" refers to the three obstacles; therefore, possessing these three, cultivation is accomplished through nature, and the perfection of the three is the natural law (*dharmatā*).
Realizing that there is neither cultivation nor nature—only the single wondrous vehicle—one is free from all discrimination, and the *dharmadhātu* becomes brilliantly clear.
This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external.

Fourth, regarding the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect: since the mind of sentient beings—the cause—already possesses the three tracks (*triyāna*), this causal fruition is named the three *nirvāṇas*. There is no distinction between cause and effect; from beginning to end, the principle is one.
If this is so, since the causal qualities are already complete, why does it not abide as the cause?
It is merely because of delusion regarding the cause that each person individually claims it to be real.
If one realizes that the nature of delusion is itself reality, then because it abides solely as the cause, after long investigating this cause, the cause manifests and is called the fruit.

It is solely because the principle of cause and effect is one; by taking this single principle as the cause, once the principle is manifested, the name of "effect" no longer exists—how could the designation of "cause" still persist?

Since both cause and effect have vanished, the nature of the principle naturally ceases to exist; it is only due to the intimacy or distance of one's wisdom that delusion results in varying degrees of depth.

Because delusion varies in its density, the three afflictions are forcibly distinguished; in meaning, this opens up the six stages of realization (*liu ji*), which are termed the varying depths of wisdom.

Thus, through diligent effort as if in a dream, the name "delusion" vanishes in emptiness; when the causal conditions of illusion are fulfilled, the fruit is perfected like a mirror-image. Although the empty image and the actual image are identical in principle, the empty one is void while the image is real. Because the image is real, it is said that the Principle is inherently present; because the empty one is void, delusion transforms into the nature. Thus, while non-dual, they are established as dual to distinguish cause and effect; yet while dual, they are non-dual, for their essence is one from beginning to end.

If one claims that the cause is different from the effect, then the cause would not truly be a cause; it is only when one understands that the effect arises from the cause that the cause can truly produce the effect.

Thus, when the three thousand realms exist within the principle, they are collectively termed "ignorance" (avidyā); when the three thousand realms have achieved fruition, they are all called "eternal bliss."
The three thousand [realms] undergo no change; ignorance is itself enlightenment. The three thousand are simultaneously eternal, with both essence and function being coextensive.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature.

Fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity: if one realizes that from time immemorial consciousness is the dharma-nature functioning as ignorance, then one can now understand that ignorance is itself the dharma-nature.

When the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and ignorance (avidyā) universally produce all dharmas, it is termed "defilement"; when ignorance and the nature of phenomena universally respond to various conditions, it is designated as "purity."

Turbid water and clear water are no different in their waves and moisture; although clarity and turbidity arise from conditions, turbidity is fundamentally inherent. Though turbidity is fundamentally inherent, it is entirely clear in its essence. Because the principle of the two waves is pervasive and their entire substance is functional activity, the three thousandfold world of cause and effect is collectively termed "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Delusion and awakening, as dependent origination, do not depart from the kṣaṇa; the nature of the kṣaṇa is eternal, and the principle of dependent origination is one. Within this single principle, purity and defilement are distinguished: specifically, there are six defiled lands and four pure lands; generally, however, all ten lands encompass both the pure and the defiled.

Therefore, one knows that the substance of defilement in every instant is entirely pure; yet, because the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested, the substance remains obscured by delusion. Thus, in the stage of semblance, the six sense organs achieve universal illumination.
This illumination divides the ten realms, each of which is clearly and vividly perceived. How could a person whose six organs are purified claim that these ten realms are fixed as ten?
The division of the true and the descent of traces in the ten realms are likewise so;

even unto the perfection of the fruit, they are equal to those hundred realms. Therefore, from the first moment of mind, one must both negate and illumine: because of illumination, the three thousand [realms] are eternally present; because of negation, they are naturally within emptiness. Throughout the day they are simultaneously absent and simultaneously manifest; without moving from this thought, one responds universally and without fixed direction, bestowing according to the response until purity and impurity are both obliterated.
Because both purity and defilement have perished, one relies upon emptiness and the Middle Way; yet, through this emptiness and the Middle Way, one transforms defilement into purity.
Since both defilement and purity are seen to vanish of their own accord within emptiness, this is established by way of the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect.

Sixth, regarding the Gate of the Non-duality of the Environment and the Embodiment: Having already realized that the Dharma-realm (zhé'ān) and the single mind are an identical non-duality, this is fundamentally due to the three thousand realms within a single thought-moment from time immemorial.

Within these three thousand realms, the two thousand realms of the five aggregates constitute the "embodiment" (zhèng), while the one thousand realms of the land belong to the "environment" (yī). Since both environment and embodiment reside within a single mind, how could this single mind be divided into subject and object?

Although there is neither subject nor object, the environment and its inhabitants remain distinct and clear; thus, within the stages of rational nature, names, and contemplative practice, there already exists the non-dual characteristic of environment and inhabitants, which causes the causes and effects of self and others to mutually encompass one another.
However, although sentient beings abide within the principle (*li*) and their fruition has not yet been realized, everything is none other than the wondrous realm of Vairocana.

Yet one must further understand that the essence-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas is pervasive though not [merely] pervasive, and the rational nature (*tathatā*) of sentient beings is localized though not [merely] localized. It remains unchanged from beginning to end; there is no obstruction between the "great" and the "small. Since cause and effect share the same principle, what distinction could there be between the environment and its inhabitants?

Therefore, pure and defiled lands, superior and inferior bodies—the phenomenal body and the Dharma-body are equal in measure; the dusty realm and the Land of Tranquil Light are no different. Thus, every single dust-mote land is all lands, and every single dust-mote body is all bodies; their breadth and narrowness, superiority and inferiority, are inconceivable, and their pure and defiled locations are inexhaustible. If it were not for the Three Thousand Worlds of Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle, how could such sovereign function be accomplished?
In this way, one comes to know that sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, and that their respective phenomena and principles mutually encompass one another.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity.
Seventh, regarding the gate of the non-duality of self and others: benefiting others according to their capacities, such activity relies upon the fundamental source.
Fundamentally, it is said that the single nature is fully endowed with both self and other; only upon reaching the stage of fruition does the self immediately benefit others.

This is like the three virtues, the three truths, and the three thousand realms within the rational nature: while one's own practice resides solely within the void, the three thousand realms for the benefit of others reach out to all things.

The infinite capacities of sentient beings do not transcend the three thousand worlds; though the means of response are numerous, they do not transcend the ten realms. The transformations and manifestations within each realm do not transcend a single thought-moment; the mutual generation of lands does not transcend the land of serene light.

Sentient beings are able to evoke [the response] because they inherently possess the three thousand realms; the Buddhas are able to respond because they have perfected the principle of the three thousand realms. Thus, the response is universal and the capacity is universal, meeting with perfect harmony and without error.
Otherwise, how could it manifest images like a mirror?

A mirror possesses the principle of manifesting images, and a form possesses the nature of producing an image; if a single form could not manifest an image when facing it, then the principle of the mirror would be exhausted and the function of the form would be obstructed.
If there were a barrier between the object and the mirror, such a principle might exist; however, there is no form that faces a mirror and yet fails to produce a reflection.

If the mirror does not manifest a reflection because it is obscured by dust, and the removal of that dust is achieved by a person polishing it—yet the manifestation of the reflection itself has no relation to the act of polishing—by means of this analogy, the general purport of contemplating the Dharma can be understood.

One should know that although the principle is inherently complete within both self and others, it must rely upon the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the cognitive cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) to function as the merit of benefiting others.

Furthermore, it is only through the unification of these conditions, the cognitive cause, and the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) that one can, in accordance with that nature, provisionally establish the myriad phenomena; thus, the self-nature does not arise, yet transformation manifests without fixed location.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants.

Eighth, regarding the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas: within the context of transforming others, these are divided into the three secrets. These receive different names according to the nature of phenomena; the mind-wheel discerns the capacities of beings, while the other two wheels establish the transformation. In manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma, there has never been even a hair’s breadth of discrepancy.
Regarding the person, they are divided into the Real (Dharmakāya) and the Responsive (Nirmāṇakāya); regarding the Dharma, they are divided into the Provisional and the Real.
If the two bodies were different, why would it be said that they are "identical to the Dharmakāya"?
If the two teachings were contradictory, why would it be said that "all attain the Buddha-way"?
If there were only the Dharma-body, it would not descend into the world;
if there were only the Buddha-way, who would bestow the three vehicles?

Since even the body is no body, what is preached is certainly not preaching. Body and speech are equal, identical to that mental wheel; mind and form are as one, transforming without deliberation. Constantly merging with the ultimate, it acts according to the capacities of things—is this not the single mind within the ten realms?
There is no realm that is not comprised of the three karmas; since even a single moment of a realm contains them, how could the three karmas be distinct?
When the function of the fruit is unimpaired, the cause must correspond to that fruit. If one believes in cause and effect, only then will one know that the Three Mysteries have their foundation.
Since the three karmas of the hundred realms are all simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle, they respond universally according to what is appropriate as the fruit.
Every manifested form and every spoken sound is fully endowed with the three karmas of the hundred realms; this is what is meant by "an emanation further creating emanations."

Therefore, within a single thought-moment of ordinary mind, there already exists the ocean-like array of the three mysteries of the rational nature; even a single speck of dust of retributive form shares the same fundamental principle as Vairocana—only then can it be called the non-differentiation of the three.
This is established through the gate of the non-duality of self and other.

Ninth is the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real: the Great Wisdom of equality constantly mirrors the Dharma-realm. This is also due to the rational nature wherein there are nine provisional aspects and one real aspect; yet the real further comprises the nine realms, and the provisional is likewise so. The provisional and the real are mutually merged; within a single thought-moment, the hundred realms are beyond discrimination, spontaneously and eternally as they are.

The attainment of the fruit arises from acceding to the fundamental principle of oneness; it is neither provisional nor real, yet it is both provisional and real. This is precisely as previously described regarding the sovereign mastery of the mind-wheel, which causes the body and speech to respond to the capacities of beings according to what is provisional and what is real.
In a single thought-moment, the three karmas do not deviate from the provisional and the real; how could their application while remaining unmoving be subject to separation or distinction?

When spoken of in relation to one another, they are designated as the provisional and the real; when considered in terms of the person, they are named the True and the Responsive. In principle, the three karmas are identical, for the provisional and the real are in profound union.
This is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the three karmas. Tenth, regarding the gate of the non-duality of receiving moisture:

the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally endowed with both the provisional and the real. Since beginningless time, habitual perfuming has been either provisional or real; yet, while the provisional and the real arise from perfuming, the principle itself remains eternally equal. When meeting with the appropriate conditions, these form habits that are supported by practice and vows. If there were no fundamental cause, even perfuming would be in vain. While what is encountered through perfuming appears diverse, this is not due to any difference in their inherent nature.

Although their nature is without distinction, they must necessarily rely on illusion to manifest. There is illusory capacity and illusory response, illusory resonance and illusory arrival; yet both the capacity to respond and those who are transformed are neither provisional nor ultimate.

Nevertheless, because sentient beings possess that which is neither provisional nor ultimate, they become the provisional and ultimate capacity for awakening; likewise, the Buddha possesses as fruition that which is neither provisional nor ultimate, thereby becoming the provisional and ultimate response. When the capacity of beings and the response accord, the bodies and lands are without partiality; they are identical to the eternally quiescent light, wherein there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.

Thus we know that the three thousand realms are co-present within the mind-ground; they are no different from the three thousand realms of the Buddha’s mind-ground. The essence of the four subtle elements is identical, and their provisional and ultimate aspects are equal in benefit.
This is established by the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the ultimate.
Therefore, through these ten gates, each gate provides universal entry; this applies equally to form and mind, even down to their receiving of moisture.

Thus, the ten subtleties (daśa-miā) are one in principle from beginning to end. Just as the objective realm inherently possesses the three [subtleties], so too does understanding arise based on that principle—this is called "wisdom" (jñāna). Wisdom and understanding guide practice; when practice and understanding accord with the principle, the three dharmas coincide. Though they are not different, they appear as different; yet, provisional designations of shallow and deep are established to define their positions and avoid confusion.
The three dharmas are simply the realization of those three principles; the subsequent five chapters concern the arising of the function of these three dharmas.
Since they constitute the "three thousand in a single thought" as emptiness, provisional existence, and the middle, their function is established.
If one understands a single thought-moment, the fundamental and manifested traces of the Dharma of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time are not remote.
Therefore, I shall again set forth ten gates so that the practice of contemplation may be recognized.
Since the title is thus, the specific may be viewed as the general; the correspondence between principle and phenomena can be understood.
The Ten Gates of Non-duality concludes.
